correctness.rationale: Reconstructed exact gap density and finite-interval RSA recursion and derived the fixed-ratio limit by uniform dominated convergence and bounded Riemann sums. Derived the local derivative recurrence (m-1)d_m=2d_(m-1), d_1=1, and transferred it through a positive smooth kernel, giving the nonzero exact coefficient. The continuum formula analytically matches the published interval 1<L<=2. Independently replayed finite-difference and discrete-rod quadrature checks from the actual CHECK.py file. The proof addresses all integers; the numerical tests only diagnose finite cases. Limits are fixed L>1 and thermodynamic substrate limit first.

originality.rationale: Closest exact primary work openly restricts the continuum fixed-ratio result to L<=2 and proposes L>2 for investigation. Competitive binary adsorption and related discrete single-stage gap calculations do not logically cover the staged all-ratio continuum expression or precise derivative-jump hierarchy. Statement-level comparisons of hypotheses and conclusions, including original full text, revealed no covering result; publication priority may still be uncertain.
residual_risks: An obscure exact formula for staged parking or an alternative gap-function transform could implicitly encode the entire continuum function and smoothness classification under different names.
Reeve-Wattis competitive mixture p->0+ asymptotics were inspected but a separate proof of an interchange of its rare-short-species and large-rod limits has not been established.
Search coverage does not prove uniqueness or publication priority; independent expert literature review is outstanding.

value.rationale: The original primary article explicitly calls for the fixed-ratio L>2 staged limit. The new theorem solves the complete natural ratio range and identifies an infinite exact, positive, successively higher-order threshold hierarchy tied to the maximum number of small rods a former vacancy can accept. This is a structural response law, not a routine numerical special case, and is useful for sharp deposition-response predictions.
